content: Oxacillin is an antibiotic commonly used to treat infections caused by specific types of bacteria. However, it is not effective against all infections, as some bacteria may have developed resistance to it. Oxacillin is only effective against bacterial infections and will not work for viral infections such as the common cold, influenza, or coronavirus. Using oxacillin or any antibiotic unnecessarily can lead to antibiotic resistance, making it less effective for future bacterial infections. It may also be prescribed for other conditions as determined by your healthcare provider. Oxacillin works by killing certain bacteria by preventing them from forming their cell walls, which are essential for their survival. Oxacillin is typically administered as an injection into a muscle or a blood vessel. It is available in the following dosage forms: 1 g injection, 2 g injection, 10 g injection, 20 mg/mL injection, and 40 mg/mL injection. It is usually given by a healthcare provider in a hospital or clinic setting. The most common side effects of oxacillin include pain, swelling, and inflammation at the injection site, as well as rash. If these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. There may be other side effects not listed here, so contact your healthcare provider if you suspect you are experiencing any adverse effects. Serious side effects of oxacillin, though less common, include severe allergic reactions, seizures, kidney damage, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, blood disorders, and liver damage. If you experience any of the following symptoms, stop using oxacillin and seek immediate medical attention: 1. Severe Allergic Reactions: Symptoms include difficulty breathing, wheezing, rapid heartbeat, fever, swollen lymph nodes, swelling of the face, lips, mouth, tongue, or throat, trouble swallowing, throat tightness, itching, hives, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting, stomach cramps, or joint pain. 2. Seizures: Symptoms may include muscle twitching, jerking, spasms, tremors, stiffening of the arms and legs, confusion, anxiety, dizziness, or loss of consciousness. 3. Kidney Damage: Symptoms include reduced urination, swelling in the feet, ankles, or legs, unusual tiredness, chest pain, difficulty breathing, confusion, nausea, or seizures. 4. Antibiotic-Associated Diarrhea: This condition, caused by an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), can occur even up to two months after stopping the antibiotic. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in the stool, severe stomach cramps, or fever. 5. Blood Disorders: Oxacillin can cause conditions such as eosinophilia, agranulocytosis, neutropenia, or bone marrow suppression. Symptoms include fever, shortness of breath, pale or yellowish skin, easy bruising or bleeding, frequent infections, unusual tiredness, dizziness, headaches, or an abnormal heartbeat. 6. Liver Damage: Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, fever, weakness, itching, loss of appetite, light-colored stool, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Certain individuals should not use oxacillin, including those allergic to oxacillin, penicillin, or any of the ingredients in the product. Your pharmacist can provide a list of ingredients if needed. Before using oxacillin, inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions, including allergies to penicillin or other medications, asthma, liver or kidney problems, or a history of antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Additionally, disclose all prescription and over-the-counter medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and supplements you are taking, as oxacillin may interact with other drugs, such as tetracyclines or probenecid. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, inform your healthcare provider, as it is not known how oxacillin may affect pregnancy or an unborn baby. Similarly, if you are breastfeeding or planning to breastfeed, let your provider know, as oxacillin passes into breast milk. There are no known interactions between oxacillin and food or drinks. However, heavy alcohol consumption may weaken your immune response and make it harder for your body to fight infections. If you accidentally use too much oxacillin, seek immediate medical help, call 911, or contact a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, unless it is almost time for your next dose. Do not double up on doses. It is important to complete the full prescribed course of oxacillin, even if your symptoms improve, to reduce the risk of antibiotic resistance. Common brand names for oxacillin include Bactocill and Prostaphlin.
